messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 48

He is a 56-year-old Middle Eastern man who has spent much of his adult life learning how to read a room quickly. It serves him well in his work as a social media manager, where tone can shift in minutes and a single post can invite praise, ridicule, or outrage. Before the trauma, he describes himself as steady, diplomatic, the one in his family who could calm everybody down. He is married, the father of grown children, and he takes pride in being reliable. He says that for most of his life he believed that if he stayed respectful, worked hard, and kept his head down, trouble would pass him by.

The event that divides his life into before and after happens two years ago, on an ordinary evening drive home. He is pulled over a few blocks from his neighborhood. At first he assumes it is a routine stop. He remembers lowering the window, keeping both hands visible on the steering wheel, already rehearsing the polite phrases he has used since immigrating as a young man. But the officer’s voice is sharp from the start. He is told to get out of the car. When he asks why, the question seems to make things worse. Within seconds, he is pushed against the vehicle. He remembers the metal pressing into his cheek, one arm twisted painfully behind his back, another officer shouting instructions that come too fast to follow. He tries to explain, tries to say he is not resisting, but his words disappear under the noise. A knee drives into his leg and he goes down hard. In his memory, what remains most vivid is not only the pain but the humiliation: people watching, phones lifted, his own breath turning ragged as he realizes he is no longer being treated as a man with a name but as a threat to be controlled.

He is released later without charges, after what he calls “hours that felt like another country.” His wife picks him up. He tells her he is fine before he begins shaking so hard he cannot get the seatbelt fastened. That night he does not sleep. Every time he closes his eyes he is back on the pavement, hearing commands, feeling the confusion of trying to obey while being overpowered. In the days that follow, bruises bloom across his arms and ribs. People tell him to file complaints, to go public, to let it go, to be grateful he came home alive. He feels all of these reactions pressing on him at once and finds that none of them touch the main thing: since that night, the world feels suddenly volatile and unsafe.

At work, the trauma folds cruelly into his daily responsibilities. He manages accounts for small businesses and community organizations, and his screen fills each day with arguments, breaking news, viral clips, public outrage. Videos of police encounters begin appearing everywhere, often without warning. Sometimes a thumbnail alone is enough to make his chest seize. He clicks away, then feels foolish, then angry at himself for being unable to do a job he has done for years. He starts muting words, avoiding comment sections, delegating tasks he used to handle easily. He keeps multiple browser tabs open so he can switch away quickly if a clip begins with flashing lights or shouted commands. His coworkers notice he is more withdrawn in meetings. He says less, second-guesses posts, worries constantly about “drawing attention.” The speed and unpredictability that once made him good at his job now leave him exhausted.

At home, his wife notices changes before he can name them. He checks the locks repeatedly at night. If a siren passes on the street, his whole body goes still. He avoids driving after dark and takes longer routes to bypass the intersection where he was stopped. When he does see a police car in traffic, his mouth dries, his hands tighten on the wheel, and he begins scanning for exits. He sleeps in fragments. Some nights he jerks awake soaked in sweat, already halfway out of bed, his heart pounding as if the officers are in the room. Other nights he does not dream but lies alert until dawn, listening for sounds outside. His wife reaches for him in sleep and he startles so sharply that she apologizes, though he is the one who feels ashamed.

He talks less with friends. He declines gatherings he once enjoyed because crowded restaurants, sudden laughter behind him, even the scrape of a chair can make him feel exposed. He has become more irritable with the people he loves, especially when they tell him he should not let “one bad incident” define him. Part of him agrees and despises himself for failing. Another part is furious that they do not understand that his fear is not abstract. It lives in his body. It appears before thought, in the tightening of his chest, the heat in his face, the need to keep watching the door.

What troubles him most now is the change in how he sees himself. He says he used to move through the world with dignity. Now he feels perpetually braced, as if some essential trust has been stripped away. He still goes to work, still pays bills, still jokes with his wife sometimes over morning coffee. From the outside, much of his life remains intact. But he lives with the sense that danger can erupt without reason, and that ordinary acts—driving home, answering a question, reaching for a wallet—can become catastrophic in an instant.
